name: Ora ora gyaru

card.summary: A masculine Japanese gyaru substyle blending biker and yanki gang aesthetics with gyaru makeup, giving a tough, streetwear-driven look.

quick.overview:
Ora ora gyaru is a substyle of the Japanese gyaru fashion subculture that borrows from bosozoku biker and yanki (delinquent) culture. It is known for tracksuits, more denim and a more masculine silhouette, combined with gyaru makeup.

The appearance payoff is a distinctive, assertive style identity: women and men who adopt it use clothing, hair and makeup choices to project a rebellious, edgy presence. It is a fashion look rather than a physical change.
quick.how: People build the look with sporty or tracksuit-style clothes and denim, gyaru-style makeup and hair, and sometimes tattoos and piercings. Descriptions also link it to riding bikes and mechanic work, and to the magazine Soul Sister.
quick.risks: As a clothing and makeup style it carries no physical risk beyond the usual cosmetics and piercing considerations.

lead: Ora ora gyaru, also called ora kei, is a gyaru substyle that combines biker gang, bosozoku and yanki influences with gyaru makeup and style. It is often confused with ane gyaru.[1]

Its signature look includes tracksuits, more denim and a more masculine silhouette. Wearers are described as rebellious and edgy, sometimes riding bikes, working as mechanics or having tattoos and piercings.[1]
The gyaru subculture itself has a history running from 1970s slang through the 1990s kogal and ganguro boom, to a more diverse, social-media-driven scene in the Reiwa era.[1]

angle.text: The style gives a styled, masculine-leaning look through clothing and gyaru makeup. It works as an identity choice rather than altering facial structure.

paras: Gyaru is a Japanese fashion subculture whose name comes from the English slang 'gal', known for dramatic makeup, dyed hair and decorated nails.[1] Ora ora gyaru layers bosozoku and yanki imagery onto this base.[1]

Other gyaru substyles include ganguro, with deep tanned skin and bleached hair, which peaked in the late 1990s and early 2000s.[1] In recent years, the broader gyaru look has shifted toward lighter makeup and softer, less rule-bound styling.[1]
